Supreme People's Court

Annual Report on Intellectual Property Cases

(2008)

Preface

The Intellectual Property Tribunal of the Supreme People’s Court is responsible for hearing all types of intellectual property civil disputes accepted by this Court, as well as certain patent and trademark grant and confirmation administrative disputes. In 2008, the Intellectual Property Tribunal of the Supreme People’s Court newly accepted a total of 277 intellectual property cases, including disputes over patent infringement, copyright infringement, trademark infringement, unfair competition, various intellectual property contracts, and patent and trademark grant and confirmation disputes. Adding the 52 cases carried over from 2007, the Tribunal heard a total of 329 cases throughout the year, an increase of 103.9% compared to 2007. By lawfully performing its intellectual property trial duties, the Supreme People’s Court resolved various intellectual property disputes and fully protected the lawful rights and interests of the parties. At the same time, through adjudication of a series of difficult, complex, and new types of intellectual property cases, the Supreme People’s Court continuously clarified relevant issues of legal application, maintaining the uniformity of judicial standards for intellectual property. The explanations of legal application issues in these intellectual property cases adjudicated by the Supreme People’s Court are of guiding and referential significance for the intellectual property judicial protection work of courts nationwide. To timely summarize trial experience, strengthen trial supervision and guidance, and promote the unification and improvement of standards for intellectual property legal application, the Intellectual Property Tribunal of the Supreme People’s Court selected ruling summaries from 23 typical cases among the 184 cases concluded in 2008, forming this Annual Report, which is hereby publicly released.

I. Intellectual Property Civil Cases

(A) Patent Cases

1. In the retrial review case of Strix Limited v. Ningbo Shengilda Electric Manufacturing Co., Ltd. and Huapu Supermarket Co., Ltd. regarding a patent infringement dispute, the Supreme People’s Court, in its Notice of Rejection of Retrial Application (2007) Min San Jian Zi No. 51-1, held that the application of the defense of prior art (defense of existing technology) only requires comparing whether all technical features of the accused infringing product that are allegedly within the scope of protection of the patent right are identical or equivalent to the corresponding technical features of other prior art technical solutions already disclosed. The application of the principle of the defense of prior art (defense of existing technology) cannot be excluded simply because the accused infringing product is identical to the patentee’s patent.

2. In the case concerning a request for instructions from the Liaoning High People’s Court on whether the conduct of Chaoyang Xingnuo Company in designing and constructing in accordance with the industry standard “Composite Foundation Dynamic Compaction Pile Design Specification” issued by the Ministry of Construction, thereby implementing the patented technology in the standard, constituted patent infringement, the Supreme People’s Court issued a Reply Letter (2008) Min San Ta Zi No. 4. The Reply held that, given the actual situation that China’s standard-setting bodies have not yet established a system for the public disclosure and use of patent information in standards, if a patentee participated in the formulation of the standard or consented to the inclusion of its patent in a national, industry, or local standard, then the patentee is deemed to have granted a license to others to implement the patent while implementing the standard. The relevant implementation conduct of others does not constitute patent infringement as defined in Article 11 of the Patent Law. The patentee may request the implementer to pay a certain usage fee, but the amount paid shall be significantly lower than a normal license fee. If the patentee has promised to waive the usage fee, such promise shall be honored.

3. In the retrial review case concerning a dispute over usage fees during the provisional protection period of a patent for invention and a dispute over infringement of a patent for invention, as well as a jurisdictional objection, between Zhejiang Hangzhou Xinfu Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. v. Shandong Xinfa Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Aixiti International Trading Co., Ltd., the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2008) Min Shen Zi No. 81, clarified the principle for determining jurisdiction over disputes regarding usage fees during the provisional protection period of a patent for invention. The Supreme People’s Court held that although a dispute over usage fees during the provisional protection period of a patent for invention does not strictly fall within the category of patent infringement disputes, it is essentially a type of tort dispute related to patents. Therefore, jurisdiction should be determined according to the principles for determining jurisdiction in tort actions under Article 29 of the Civil Procedure Law. Such disputes are most similar in nature to patent infringement disputes. Hence, until the law or judicial interpretations make special provisions for jurisdiction in such cases, the jurisdictional rules for patent infringement disputes may be applied by analogy. Where the alleged infringing conduct spans both before and after the date of publication of the grant of the patent for invention, and the conduct is continuous and consistent before and after, for the convenience of the parties in litigation, the right holder shall be permitted to simultaneously assert claims for both the usage fee during the provisional protection period and the patent infringement.

4. In the appeal case of Lanzing Chemical New Materials Co., Ltd., Jiangxi Xinghuo Organic Silicon Plant v. Shandong Dongyue Organic Silicon Material Co., Ltd., Shandong Dongyue Fluorine Silicon Material Co., Ltd., and Beijing Petrochemical Design Institute Co., Ltd. regarding a dispute over infringement of a utility model patent, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2008) Min San Zhong Zi No. 7, held that the accepting court’s having jurisdiction over the case is a prerequisite for hearing the case. When a conflict arises between determining the litigant and determining jurisdiction, the accepting court should first make a ruling on the issue of jurisdiction.

5. In the retrial review case concerning a jurisdictional objection to a patent infringement dispute, Cai Langchun v. Foshan Shiwan Eagle Ceramics Co., Ltd., Jiangmen Xinli Plastic Factory Co., Ltd., and Zhu Genliang, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2008) Min Shen Zi No. 19, held that the Hangzhou Intermediate People’s Court had previously heard multiple infringement lawsuits filed by the retrial applicant involving the patent in question, and this case did not fall within the category of cases with significant impact within Zhejiang Province. Therefore, to facilitate the trial of the case, a superior court may, in accordance with Article 39 of the Civil Procedure Law, transfer a civil case of first instance under its jurisdiction to a lower court for trial.

(B) Copyright Cases

6. In the retrial review case of Guangdong Dasheng Cultural Communication Co., Ltd. v. Hong Ruting, Han Wei, Guangzhou Audio and Video Publisher, Chongqing Sanxia CD-ROM Development Co., Ltd., and Liansheng Commercial Chain Co., Ltd. concerning a copyright infringement dispute, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil judgment (2008) Min Ti Zi No. 51, clarified the scope of application of Article 39, Paragraph 3 and Article 41, Paragraph 2 of the Copyright Law. Article 39, Paragraph 3 of the Copyright Law establishes a statutory license system that limits the rights of music copyright owners, i.e., “a sound recording producer who uses a musical work that has been lawfully recorded as a sound recording to produce a sound recording may do so without obtaining permission from the copyright owner, but shall pay remuneration as prescribed.” Although this provision only states that the use of a musical work that has been lawfully recorded as a sound recording to produce a sound recording may be done without permission from the copyright owner, the legislative intent of this provision is to facilitate and promote the dissemination of musical works. Therefore, the reproduction and distribution of sound recordings made using such musical works should also be subject to the statutory license provided in Article 39, Paragraph 3 of the Copyright Law. That is, once a sound recording of a musical work produced with the permission of the copyright owner has been made public, if another person subsequently uses that musical work to create another sound recording and reproduces and distributes it, the provision of Article 41, Paragraph 2 requiring “permission from the copyright owner” does not apply.

7. In the retrial review case of Xinchuan Online (Beijing) Information Technology Co., Ltd. v. China Network Communications Corporation Zigong Branch concerning a dispute over infringement of the right to communicate works through information networks, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2008) Min Shen Zi No. 926, held that with respect to relevant notarized evidence submitted by the parties, the court, when necessary, may, based on the specific circumstances of the network environment and network evidence, examine whether the network information certified by the notarization originated from the Internet rather than a local computer, and determine accordingly whether it can be used as evidence for establishing the facts. Since it is technically possible to pre-set a target webpage on a local computer, so that when accessing the Internet through that computer, the virtual target webpage coexists with other real Internet pages, and when the notarial act is performed outside the notary office, the computer and mobile hard disk used for the notarization are not under the notary’s control before the notarial act, and the notarial certificate does not record whether the cleanliness of the computer and mobile hard disk was checked, the Supreme People’s Court held that although such a notarial certificate can prove that the act recorded in the certificate occurred in the presence of the notary, it is insufficient to prove that the act occurred within the Internet environment.

8. In the retrial review case of Futabasha Co., Ltd. of Japan v. Shanghai Enjia Economic and Trade Development Co., Ltd., Guangzhou Chengyi Glasses Co., Ltd., and Xiangshui County Shifu Economic Development Co., Ltd. concerning a copyright infringement dispute, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2007) Min San Jian Zi No. 14-1, held that Futabasha’s claim not only alleged that the respondents Chengyi Company and Shifu Company unlawfully used its copyrighted “Crayon Shin-chan” artwork in their registered or held trademarks, but also alleged that Enjia Company, without permission, unlawfully used its artwork in product sales and promotion. Futabasha’s lawsuit against such actual use in product sales, promotion, etc., involves a dispute over civil rights and interests. Provided that the conditions of Article 108 of the Civil Procedure Law are met, the people’s court should accept the case.

9. In the appeal case of Appellants China Federation of Literary and Art Circles Audio and Video Publisher, Tianjin Tianbao Culture Development Co., Ltd., and Tianjin Tianbao Disc Co., Ltd. v. Appellee Guangdong Changjin Audio-Video Co., Ltd. and original defendant Hebei Hebei Clapper Opera Theater et al. concerning a copyright infringement dispute, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil judgment (2008) Min San Zhong Zi No. 5, held that: First, for the performance of a complete theatrical work, since the preparation, organization, rehearsal, etc., are all conducted by the performing unit (such as a theater or troupe), and the necessary investment for the performance is also borne by the performing unit, the performance reflects the will of the performing unit. Therefore, the performing unit is the performer within the meaning of the Copyright Law. Second, the “right of a video producer” enjoyed by a video producer is different from the “right of exclusive publication and distribution of video products of the relevant repertoire” obtained through authorization from the performer and relevant copyright owners. The former refers to the rights of reproduction, distribution, rental, and communication through information networks enjoyed over video products produced by the producer itself, while the latter is similar to an exclusive publishing right, which can prohibit others from publishing or distributing video products of the same repertoire performed by the same performer without permission, without being limited to a particular performance session or a particular recording version.

10. In the retrial case of Sun Nan v. Beijing Golden Disc Co., Ltd., Zibo Yinzhuo Department Store Co., Ltd., and Jiangxi Audio and Video Publisher concerning a dispute over infringement of performer’s rights, the Supreme People’s Court entered a civil ruling (2008) Min Shen Zi No. 804 to retry the case. Although the case was concluded by granting the withdrawal of the lawsuit upon the parties’ application through civil ruling (2008) Min Ti Zi No. 55, the trial of this case unified the understanding of the parties’ burden of proof and the standards for determining relevant evidence. Regarding the determination of the performer’s identity, the color cover and disc core of the disc in question bore the words “Sun Nan Dui Shi” and “Sun Nan: Latest Album,” printed multiple photos of Sun Nan, and Sun Nan admitted that the relevant tracks were his performances. In the absence of contrary evidence to overturn this fact, Sun Nan could be identified as the performer of the relevant tracks. Regarding the determination of the infringer’s identity: First, Golden Disc Company denied that it reproduced and distributed the disc in question, but the disc had its production source identification code (SID) etched on it. Second, Golden Disc Company admitted that the relevant reproduction authorization letter submitted to the court was forged, but did not explain by whom it was forged, and did not provide a reasonable explanation for why the publication number, publication and distribution date, and related text displayed on the disc in question were consistent with another lawfully signed reproduction authorization letter. Third, Jiangxi Audio and Video Publisher argued that Golden Disc Company had previously misappropriated its publishing number without authorization. Based on the comprehensive consideration of the above evidence, it could be determined that the disc in question was reproduced and distributed by Golden Disc Company.

11. In the retrial review case of Wang Zhirong v. Hunan University Press concerning a publishing contract dispute, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2008) Min Shen Zi No. 823, held that the primary legal issue in this case was whether Article 16 of the “Regulations on Remuneration for Publishing Literary Works” formulated by the National Copyright Administration should apply. The Supreme People’s Court held that since the legal basis for this article — Article 40 of the Implementing Regulations of the Copyright Law before its revision — was deleted during the revision on September 15, 2002, although the relevant national authorities have not yet adjusted Article 16 of the said Regulations, this article is inconsistent with the spirit of the current Copyright Law of the People’s Republic of China and has become outdated; therefore, it should not be applied in this case.

12. In the retrial review case of Zhang Peilian v. Sichuan Science and Technology Press concerning a copyright infringement dispute, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2008) Min Jian Zi No. 126, clarified that if a publication has been determined by an effective judgment to be infringing and has fully compensated the right holder, then further distribution of that publication after the judgment takes effect is a matter of enforcement of the original judgment and does not constitute a new act of infringement.

(C) Trademark Cases

13. In the case concerning a request for instructions from the dispute between Shenzhen Yuanhang Technology Co., Ltd. v. Shenzhen Tencent Computer Systems Co., Ltd., Tencent Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., and Shenzhen Tencent Computer Systems Co., Ltd. Xi’an Branch over trademark infringement and unfair competition, the Supreme People’s Court, in its Reply Letter (2008) Min San Ta Zi No. 12, held that for a name of a poker game that has become established by common usage among relevant public in a certain region, if the party uses it not as a trademark to distinguish the source of goods or services, but merely as a game name reflecting the content, characteristics, etc., of such game, it may be deemed as fair use. Whether the situation falls under the above category should be determined in light of the specific circumstances of the case and in accordance with Article 49 of the Implementing Regulations of the Trademark Law.

(D) Unfair Competition Cases

14. In the retrial review case of Guangdong Weixiong Group Co., Ltd., Foshan Gaoming Zhengye Electric Industrial Co., Ltd., Guangdong Zhengye Electric Co., Ltd. v. Foshan Shunde Zhengye Electric Co., Ltd. and Foshan Shunde Guangda Enterprise Group Co., Ltd. concerning a dispute over trademark infringement and unfair competition, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2005) Min San Jian Zi No. 15-1, held that an enterprise name, especially its trade name, protected under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law is different from personality rights in the general sense. It is a commercial identifier that distinguishes different market players and may be succeeded. This ruling also clarified that registering and using text identical to another party’s registered trademark as a trade name in an enterprise name, producing and dealing in similar products, if it is sufficient to cause confusion among the relevant public as to the source of the goods, may constitute an act of unfair competition even if the other party’s trademark has not been recognized as a well-known trademark or a famous trademark.

15. In the appeal case concerning a jurisdictional objection to a dispute over trade secret infringement, Avery Dennison Corporation, Avery (Guangzhou) Co., Ltd., Avery (Kunshan) Co., Ltd., Avery (China) Co., Ltd. v. Four Pillars Enterprise Co., Ltd., Four Pillars Industrial (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., Nanhai Lishui Yili Printing Factory, and Foshan Huanshi Dongsheng Fenjiang Printing Factory Business Department, the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2007) Min San Zhong Zi No. 10, held that selling infringing products manufactured by trade secret infringement does not constitute an act of trade secret infringement as defined in Article 10 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. The place of implementation and the place of result of the act of using a trade secret are usually coincident; that is, the process of using a trade secret is generally the process of manufacturing the infringing product. When the infringing product is completed, the infringing result of using the trade secret occurs simultaneously. Therefore, the place of sale of the infringing product should not be regarded as the place where the infringing result of using the trade secret occurred.

(E) Technology Contract Cases

16. In the retrial review case concerning a jurisdictional objection to a technology commission development contract dispute, Great Wall Motor Company Limited v. Kautex (Shanghai) Plastic Products Co., Ltd., the Supreme People’s Court, in its civil ruling (2008) Min Shen Zi No. 46, held that Article 24 of the Civil Procedure Law clarifies that a court in the place of performance of a contract has jurisdiction over a lawsuit brought as a result of a contract dispute, but there are no further provisions defining the “place of performance.” The Supreme People’s Court’s Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China also do not interpret the place of performance for technology contracts. However, Chapter 4 of the Contract Law provides principles for determining the place of performance of a contract. Therefore, the place of performance of the contract as stipulated in Article 24 of the Civil Procedure Law may be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Contract Law regarding the place of performance.

II. Intellectual Property Administrative Cases

(A) Patent Grant and Confirmation Cases

1. In the retrial case on petition for administrative retrial concerning the invalidation of a patent for invention, Jinan Wuyou Boiler Factory v. the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office and the third party Shu Xuezhang, the Supreme People’s Court, in its administrative judgment (2007) Xing Ti Zi No. 4, clarified the understanding of the principle of prohibition of double patenting under patent law and the legality of related administrative operations, and also clarified the connotation of the concept of “same invention-creation” under patent law. The focus of this case was whether the relevant administrative operation established in Gazette No. 6 of the Examination Guidelines published by the former Patent Office on September 28, 1995, which allowed the same applicant to apply for both a utility model patent and an invention patent for the same invention-creation, complies with the principle of prohibition of double patenting under patent law. This also involved the validity of thousands of patents previously granted by the Patent Office based on this operation. The Supreme People’s Court held that “same invention-creation” as referred to in the Patent Law means patent applications or patents with the same scope of protection. In the method of determination, only the content claimed in each application or patent needs to be compared. The two patents involved in this case were not the same invention-creation. The prohibition of double patenting under the Patent Law means that the same invention-creation cannot have two or more effective patents existing simultaneously, not that the same invention-creation can only be granted a patent once. The relevant administrative operation did not violate the legislative intent of the prohibition of double patenting at the time of its issuance or currently.

2. In the series of retrial review cases concerning the invalidation of design patents, the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office v. Kewan Trademark Investment Co., Ltd. and Foshan Shunde Xinda Dyeing and Finishing Machinery Co., Ltd., the Supreme People’s Court, in its administrative judgments (2008) Xing Ti Zi Nos. 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8, elucidated the following opinions: Article 13, Paragraph 1 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law contains provisions on the prohibition of double patenting. For design patents, to prevent conflicts between design patent rights, whether the designs are identical or similar, and regardless of whether the applicant is the same, only one patent right shall be granted in accordance with the said administrative regulation. A patent that has been declared invalid is deemed never to have existed from the beginning and should no longer be used as a reference document for determining whether double patenting exists. If each unit design is identical, and the only difference is a simple increase or decrease in the number of units, the designs are considered similar designs.

3. In the retrial case of Rugao Aijike Textile Machinery Co., Ltd. v. Patent Reexamination Board of the National Intellectual Property Administration and Wang Yushan (third party) — dispute over invalidation of utility model patent, the Supreme People's Court's (2007) Xing Ti Zi No. 3 administrative ruling clarified two important issues: whether the filing of an enterprise standard constitutes disclosure within the meaning of the Patent Law, and whether the court may exercise judicial power to modify the decision in patent confirmation administrative cases. The Supreme People's Court held that the filing of an enterprise standard does not mean that the specific content of the standard must be publicly released to society; nor does filing mean that the public may freely access and obtain the standard. An enterprise standard does not, by virtue of the filing act alone, constitute disclosure for the purposes of the Patent Law. Under the current framework of administrative litigation law, a court lacks sufficient legal basis to directly declare the validity of the patent in issue in the main text of its judgment.

(B) Trademark Authorization and Confirmation Cases

4. In the retrial application case of Southwest Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. v. Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce and Bayer Consumer Care AG — administrative dispute over trademark, the Supreme People's Court's (2007) Xing Jian Zi No. 111-1 notice of rejection of retrial application held that generic names include legally prescribed generic names and generic names established by common practice. Names included in local pharmaceutical standards should in principle be recognized as generic names; however, if such national pharmaceutical standards are subsequently amended, they should no longer be considered legally prescribed generic names. The criterion for determining whether a name is a generic name is whether it is a term used by industry operators by common practice and in a widespread manner to designate a particular class of goods. The time point for determining a generic name should be based on the factual state at the time of review.

5. In the retrial application case of Changzhou Chenglian Power Supply Manufacturing Co., Ltd. v. Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce and Changzhou Chuanglian Power Supply Co., Ltd. — administrative dispute over trademark, the Supreme People's Court's (2006) Xing Jian Zi No. 118-1 notice of rejection of retrial application clarified that the circumstances of "obtaining registration by deceptive means or by other improper means" in Article 41(1) of the Trademark Law are listed in parallel and relate to absolute grounds for cancellation of trademark registration. In disputes over registered trademarks involving prior rights, the "other improper means" in that provision should not be applied to cancellation disputes involving private rights; rather, the provisions of Article 41(2) and (3) of the Trademark Law should apply. Meanwhile, the notice further clarified that to resolve issues of bad-faith preemptive registration of prior trademarks or other infringement of prior rights, and to curb acts of unfair competition, a correct understanding and application of Article 31 of the Trademark Law would suffice. Article 31 of the Trademark Law sets three conditions for the protection of unregistered trademarks: prior use, a certain degree of influence, and preemptive registration by improper means. Among these, "a certain degree of influence" and "improper means" are inherently flexible. The standard for requiring a certain degree of influence of a trademark should not be set too high, and may be considered in light of the registrant's knowledge or bad faith.

6. In the series of retrial application cases of Japan-based Kabushiki Kaisha Futaba Sha v. Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce and Shanghai Enjia Economic and Trade Development Company — administrative disputes over trademark, the Supreme People's Court's (2007) Min San Jian Zi Nos. 25-1, 26-1, 27-1, 28-1, 29-1, 30-1, 31-1, 32-1, and 33-1 notices of rejection of retrial application held that, pursuant to Article 31 of the Trademark Law and other provisions, a request to cancel a registered trademark on the ground that its registration infringes prior copyright or other rights must be filed within five years from the date of registration of that trademark. There is no legal basis for the determination that the five-year period prescribed in the Trademark Law should be calculated from December 1, 2001, the effective date of the Trademark Law.

7. In the retrial application case of Yunnan Dianhong Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd. v. Shantou Kangwang Fine Chemical Industry Co., Ltd. and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce — administrative dispute over trademark, the Supreme People's Court's (2007) Xing Jian Zi No. 184-1 notice of rejection of retrial application clarified that "use" as provided in Article 44(4) of the Trademark Law refers to open, genuine, and lawful use of a trademark in commercial activities. It also indicated that the legal basis for determining whether trademark use is lawful is not limited to the Trademark Law and its supporting regulations. The use of a trademark by an operator in business activities that violate the mandatory or prohibitive provisions of laws or regulations cannot be considered as "use" within the meaning of the Trademark Law. The remedial measure of ordering rectification within a specified time limit under Article 44 of the Trademark Law does not apply to the act of ceasing use for three consecutive years under Article 44(4). Where a third party applies to the Trademark Office for cancellation of such a registered trademark, if the registrant has no evidence of actual use or the evidence is insufficient to prove actual use, and there is no justifiable reason for non-use, the registered trademark should be cancelled.
